To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

we propose an objective function that leverages the annotations of neighboring inputs to train models for tasks with sparse supervision, and that our method consistently improves over baselines across multiple tasks.

(i) we propose a new objective for training neural models that leverages the sparse annotations of neighbors to improve predictions on a given example, (ii) we demonstrate that this objective can be used in a variety of structured prediction tasks to improve performance and (iii) we show that the proposed objective can be applied to improve output diversity, an important property of models in the image-grounded sequence generation tasks we consider

we propose a new objective function for learning from sparse annotations that leverages supervision from neighbors, and that our method improves performance over maximum likelihood training in a variety of tasks.
In summary, our research is concerned with
how to learn from sparse annotations.
how we can learn from the annotations of neighbors to learn better models for multi-modal prediction tasks.
how to learn a model that can generalize well to unobserved outputs, given only a small amount of supervision.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that

the method proposed in this paper is an effective way of transferring supervision from neighboring examples in multi-modal tasks, and that it is able to improve upon standard baselines in both image-grounded sequence generation tasks and multi-label classification.
our method can learn to predict plausible but unannoted outputs from the annotations of similar inputs.
our method can be used to improve the quality of outputs of neural networks for a number of different tasks, including image captioning, question generation and multi-label classification.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
our approach is a simple yet effective method to learn multi-modal mappings from sparse annotations.
we propose a new objective function to learn multi-modal mappings from sparse annotations and show its efficacy on two image-grounded tasks.

we propose a novel method for multi-modal mapping tasks, which is based on the assumption that the annotations for neighboring examples can be transferred to the current example, and we demonstrate the effectiveness of this method in a wide range of tasks and datasets.
The main takeaway from our work is that
we can leverage the structure of the input space to improve performance on ambiguous prediction tasks.
we can improve the quality of predictions for an ambiguous task by leveraging the information from the neighbors.
, in many cases of interest, we can learn more effective models of the data by leveraging information from the neighborhood of a given example.
